title: Family feuds
hookLine: old feuds cost more each year

lines: THE REASON FADES. THE SILENCE STAYS.
cards: A chair at the holiday table that nobody sits in anymore. A cousin who isn't invited, and nobody quite remembers why. Two sisters who send birthday messages through their mother.

Family feuds have a way of outliving their reasons. The original argument fades, and what's left is the silence, which gets heavier as it ages: one more wedding missed, one more grandchild who's never met an aunt.
A proverb has a picture for that weight, and the book of Numbers has a quarrel between three siblings, and the short sentence that began to end it.

teach.h: HARDER TO WIN THAN A STRONG CITY.
teach.b: First, why it gets harder. Proverbs eighteen says, in the King James words: "A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle."
Every year of silence can feel like another bar across the gate. Second, the quarrel.

In the book of Numbers, Miriam and Aaron speak against their brother Moses, first about the woman he married, then about whether God speaks only through him. A family argument in the middle of the wilderness camp.
In the story, Miriam is suddenly struck with leprosy, and Moses, the one spoken against, is the one who cries out for her: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee."
In Hebrew, the plea is five words long. No speech about who was right, no demand for an apology first. Just: let my sister be well.
Miriam has to stay outside the camp for seven days, and the text adds: "the people journeyed not till Miriam was brought in again." A whole people stays put until the sister is back inside.
A family quarrel can hold everyone up, and the step that starts to end one can be as small as five words.

how: Jews and Christians read the quarrel of Miriam, Aaron and Moses in Numbers 12; the Talmud (Berakhot 34a) points to Moses's five-word prayer for his sister as an example of a short prayer.

games.q: you're Moses. your sister and brother have spoken against you, and now your sister is struck with leprosy. what do you do?
o: say nothing: she brought it on herself.
cry out for her to be healed.
games.why: Moses, the one spoken against, pleads: "heal her now, O God, I beseech thee." five words in Hebrew, and no speech about who was right.

practice: Bring to mind one rift in your family, yours or one you're standing near, and don't try to solve it; just ask what the smallest possible step would be.
Not a speech or a reunion, but something tiny: a like on a photo, a card, a neutral hello at the next gathering, or telling the people in someone else's quarrel that you'd rather stay out of it.
Let a few options come, choose one and hold it lightly; you're only finding where the first stone is. If you pray, you can bring that family into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Family feuds. Quarrels inside a family that outlive their reasons, and the small step that can begin to end them. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Numbers 12:13: God, please, heal her, please. Five words.

carryVoice: Your line: one step. Five words began to bring Miriam back into the camp. See you tomorrow.
